newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Fund scandals delay launch of Hong Kong no-loads.
newsitem.headline: Fund scandals delay launch of Hong Kong no-loads.

text.p: Recent fund management scandals have tainted investor sentiment in Hong Kong, forcing the territory's first no-load fund management service to delay its launch, the service's chief executive said on Tuesday.

"We want to ensure that any negative press and the effect of that has disappeared before we launch our new service," said Philip Hampden-Smith, chief executive officer of Manulife Regent Investment Asia Ltd.

Manulife Regent, a 50-50 joint venture between the Canadian insurance mammoth Manulife Financial and Hong Kong's aggressive Regent Pacific Group Ltd, was set to launch its new service when London and Hong Kong regulators unveiled trading irregularities at fund managers Jardine Fleming and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"We have been concerned that there may some negative investor sentiment, particularly in the retail sense," Hampden-Smith said.

Regulators late last month revoked the authorisation of Jardine Fleming's London-based subsidiary following revelations of late allocation of trades by a senior fund manager at the company's Hong Kong-based Jardine Fleming Investment Management.
That scandal was quickly followed by revelations of suspected irregular investments in unlisted stocks by three European funds managed by Morgan Grenfell Asset Management.
Jardine Fleming is equally held by the Jardine Matheson and Robert Fleming groups, while Morgan Grenfell is part of the Deutsche Bank group.

Hampden-Smith declined to say how long he thinks it will take for the dust to settle sufficiently to allow the launch of Hong Kong's first set of no-load funds, which will charge a management fee of between 0.25 and 1.50 percent.
No-load funds, common in the United Kingdom and North America, have yet to catch on in Hong Kong's retail market which is dominated by Jardine Fleming.
Manulife Regent acquired Regent's retail fund management assets, valued at US$70 million, shortly after it was set up five months ago.
Manulife Financial manages C$45 billion in insurance assets and held a majority stake last year in Altamira, one of Canada's newest and most aggressive mutual fund managers.
